posts.title: The Doors of Perception and Heaven and Hell
posts.description: This is the book from which Jim Morrison’s band took its name. The title comes from a line by the English visionary and poet, William Blake: “If the doors of perception were cleansed every thing would appear to man as it is, infinite.” Huxley decides to test Blake’s theory by dosing himself on mescaline, the hallucinogenic ingredient in peyote. posts.title: In the Café of Lost Youth
posts.description: In the Café of Lost Youth opens in the Condé café in Paris in the 1950s. The narrator of the opening chapter, a student in his early twenties, introduces us to some of the café’s regulars, men and women of varying ages who all seem to be adrift. posts.title: A History of Western Philosophy
posts.description: Coming from Aldous Huxley’s The Perennial Philosophy to Bertrand Russel’s A History of Western Philosophy is an interesting transition. Both men have tremendous knowledge and intellect, but they are very different writers.
